# A triangle frustum with a unique deepest point and deficient active normals

This is an actual all-halfspace certificate. It disproves an unconditional finite active-normal KKT assertion for a smooth secondary objective at a deepest point. It does not contradict a depth bound or establish an OC counterexample. A product construction at the end gives the same obstruction for an actual mixed body.

Let

    T=conv{(2,−1),(−1,2),(−1,−1)},
    K_ε={(x,t): −1≤t≤1, x∈(1+εt)T},
    0<ε≤10^(−9).

Its defining inequalities are affine, so this is a full-dimensional compact convex triangle frustum. Put

    γ=4/9,    t_*=ε/3,    y_*=(0,t_*).

**Theorem.** The unique ordinary deepest point of K_ε is y_*. Its normalized depth is exactly 4/9. The only oriented active halfspace normals at this point are positive multiples of

    (1,0,0),  (0,1,0),  (−1,−1,0).                    (1)

The minimizing projective parameter at y_* is a nonzero vertical vector. Hence the gradient of projective energy, or its positive d-th root, is not in the cone or linear span of the active halfspace normals.

The all-normal cap proof uses the triangle paired-tail inequality

    F_n(s)+F_n(−s)≥8/9,                               (2)

where F_n(s)=|T∩{n·x≥s}|/|T|. Section 1a supplies a self-contained elementary proof, independently derived by Two-sided during the audit. Thus no localization theorem or external equality classification is required. The broader archived result in `candidate 732b11a769399016` is consistent with this direct special case.

## 1. Elementary triangle formulas

For every nonzero horizontal normal n, scale it so that the largest of its three vertex values is 2. Since the vertex values sum to zero, after sorting the other two they are

    2,  −R,  R−2,      1≤R≤4.

Write s=R−1≥0. When 1≤R≤2, the through-zero cap isolates the maximum vertex and

    F_n(0)=4/[(2+R)(4−R)]=4/(9−s²).                  (3)

When 2≤R≤4, taking the complement of the minimum-vertex cap gives

    F_n(0)=1−R²/[(R+2)(2R−2)]≥1/2.                   (4)

The last difference from 1/2 is (R−2)/[(R+2)(2R−2)]. Thus F_n(0)≥4/9, with equality exactly when R=1. These equality normals are precisely the three in (1).

The projection n·X of a uniform point X of T has the usual piecewise affine triangular density, with maximum

    2/(R+2)≤2/3.                                     (5)

One can verify (3)–(5) by similar triangles: the upper tail in the isolated maximum-vertex regime is

    F_n(q)=(2−q)²/[(2+R)(4−R)].                       (6)

The complementary lower-vertex formula gives the second affine density segment; their common peak is (5). Repeated vertex values are their continuous limits and obey the same bound. In particular, for |s|≤1/4 and |q|≤1/4,

    F_n(q)+F_n(−q)=(8+2q²)/(9−s²).                   (7)

Only s≥0 is needed in the sorted parametrization; allowing the opposite ordering of the two lower vertices changes its sign and leaves every displayed formula unchanged.

## 1a. Elementary all-orientation paired tails

Here is the direct proof of (2), supplied by Two-sided's independent audit. Put D=(R+2)(4−R), E=(R+2)(2R−2), and q≥0.

For 1<R<2 and 0≤q≤2−R, both tails are in the upper-vertex formula, giving (8+2q²)/D≥8/9. For 2−R≤q≤R their sum is

    J(q)=1+(2−q)²/D−(R−q)²/E.

This is concave since E≤D. Its first endpoint agrees with the previous interval and is at least 8/9; its last endpoint is 1+F_n(R)≥1. For q≥R the negative-threshold tail is one, so the sum remains at least one.

For 2<R<4, the sum on 0≤q≤R−2 is 2−2(R²+q²)/E and decreases to the mixed interval. On R−2≤q≤2 it is the same J, now convex. Its minimum occurs at q=(R+2)/3, inside that interval, and equals

    2(R+4)/[3(R+2)]
      =8/9+2(4−R)/[9(R+2)]≥8/9.

On 2≤q≤R, the positive-threshold tail is zero and the other increases, so no smaller value occurs. Afterwards their sum is one. Finally R=1,2,4 follow by continuity of actual triangle cap volume in its nonzero normal and threshold, including all supporting thresholds. This proves (2) for every orientation and every shift.

## 2. A uniform exact gap for the product body

For ε=0 and source (0,0), the cap with normal (n,β) has fraction

    P_0(n,β)= (1/2)∫_0^1 [F_n(βt)+F_n(−βt)]dt.       (8)

Equation (2) proves P_0≥γ. We need a UNIFORM strict gap away from neighborhoods of (1). Define

    Δ=4/1287,
    δ=Δ²/192=1/(12·1287²)=1/19,876,428.              (9)

For nonzero n in the normalization of Section 1, the local neighborhoods will be

    s≤1/4 and |β|≤1/4.                               (10)

Every normal outside their union has

    P_0(n,β)≥γ+δ.                                    (11)

Here is a complete quantitative proof.

If |β|≥72, then |n·X|≤4 and the cap contains an interval of heights of length at least 1−4/|β|. Consequently P_0≥(1−4/|β|)/2≥17/36=γ+1/36.

Suppose |β|≤72 and s≥1/4. Equations (3)–(4) give F_n(0)≥γ+Δ; the endpoint identity is 64/143−4/9=4/1287. The density bound (5) gives

    F_n(βt)+F_n(−βt)≥2F_n(0)−(4/3)|β|t.

For 0≤t≤Δ/96 the right side is at least 2γ+Δ. On the rest of [0,1] use (2). Inserting into (8) gives an excess at least Δ²/192=δ.

Finally suppose s<1/4 and 1/4≤|β|≤72. For 0≤t≤1/(4|β|), formula (7) applies and gives an excess above 2γ of at least 2β²t²/9. Use (2) elsewhere. Its contribution to (8) is

    β²/9 ∫_0^(1/(4|β|)) t²dt
       =1/(1728|β|)≥1/124,416>δ.

A pure vertical normal has P_0=1/2 and also satisfies (11). This proves the uniform gap, with no compactness-only estimate left unspecified.

## 3. Uniform comparison to the actual frustum

Put r(t)=1+εt and I_2=∫_(−1)^1r(t)²dt=2(1+ε²/3). The change of variables x=r(t)X identifies normalized volume on K_ε with uniform X∈T and the independent height density r(t)²/I_2. For a cap through y_*, its affine margin is

    n·X+βt + ε[t n·X−β/3].                            (12)

For every normal, including pure vertical normals, and 0≤ε≤1/2,

    |P_ε(n,β;y_*)−P_0(n,β)|≤8ε.                     (13)

To verify this uniformly, first let n≠0 and normalize as above. Under the product law the unperturbed margin S=n·X+βt has density at most

    min(2/3,1/(2|β|)),

with the first bound alone at β=0. The perturbation in (12) has absolute value at most ε(4+|β|/3). A changed cap indicator must therefore lie in the corresponding symmetric band about S=0. Its product probability is at most

    ε(4+|β|/3) min(4/3,1/|β|) ≤(17/3)ε.

The last bound follows by splitting at |β|=3/4. Separately, the ratio of the actual height density to the uniform one differs from 1 by at most

    [2ε+(2/3)ε²]/(1+ε²/3)≤(7/3)ε.

Their sum is (13). For pure vertical normals the event changes by uniform probability ε/6, and the same density-ratio estimate is more than sufficient.

Since 8·10^(−9)<δ, equations (11)–(13) show that every normal outside (10) has actual cap fraction STRICTLY greater than γ.

## 4. Exact cap formula in all local neighborhoods

For the normals in (10), every horizontal slice is in the SAME isolated-vertex regime. Indeed r≥1/2, |t−t_*|≤7/6, and |β|≤1/4. Thus the threshold −β(t−t_*) lies strictly above the two negative vertex heights and below the positive one, uniformly over all t∈[−1,1]. In particular its absolute value is at most 7/24, whereas the least negative-height magnitude is at least 3/8.

Equation (6) therefore gives the exact normalized fraction

    P_ε(n,β;y_*)
      = [∫_(−1)^1 (2r(t)+β(t−t_*))²dt]
                              /[(9−s²)I_2].          (14)

The choice t_*=ε/3 gives ∫r(t)(t−t_*)dt=0. Also

    ∫(t−t_*)²dt=I_2/3.

Hence (14) simplifies to the particularly rigid formula

    P_ε(n,β;y_*)=(4+β²/3)/(9−s²)≥4/9.               (15)

Equality holds exactly when s=0 and β=0. Together with the strict all-normal exterior gap, this proves the depth and the complete active-normal statement. Halfspaces containing y_* but with boundary not through it have strictly larger mass than their parallel through-y_* cap, because y_* is interior to K_ε. Thus they do not add active caps.

To prove uniqueness of the deepest point, consider any (x,t_0)∈K_ε. If x≠0, at least one of the three canonical horizontal forms n_i·x is positive, because they sum to zero and span R². Its cap through (x,t_0) has a strictly smaller slice mass than its through-axis counterpart at every height, so its total fraction is strictly below γ.

If x=0 and t_0≠t_*, use a canonical horizontal normal with a sufficiently small vertical tilt. The same isolated-vertex formula now has linear β coefficient proportional to

    ∫r(t)(t−t_0)dt=2(t_*−t_0)≠0.

A small tilt of the appropriate sign strictly reduces the cap fraction below γ. At the two endpoint heights a horizontal supporting plane already has zero volume, or the same small-tilt argument applies. Thus y_* is the unique deepest point in the whole body.

## 5. Exact local depth along the missing vertical direction

Write t_0=t_*+h. Set g_0=δ−8·10^(−9)>0, and restrict, for example, to

    |h|<h_0=min(1/48,g_0/12).

Then the ACTUAL depth is

    depth_(K_ε)(0,t_0)
      =4/9−4h²/[9(1+ε²/3)(1/3+t_0²)].               (16)

First, uniformly over all normals and ε≤1/2, moving the source height by h changes its cap fraction by at most 6|h|. For |β|≤4, condition on t and use the horizontal density bound 2/[3r(t)]≤4/3; a threshold displacement |βh| costs at most (16/3)|h|. For |β|≥4, condition on X in (12). The height coefficient has magnitude at least |β|−2≥|β|/2, and the actual height density is at most 9/8. This costs at most (9/4)|h|. Pure vertical caps satisfy the latter estimate directly. Thus the exterior cap gap remains at least g_0/2 under the displayed restriction.

Inside (10), the isolated-vertex formula still holds for |h|≤1/48: the threshold magnitude is at most (1/4)(1+1/6+1/48)<3/8. Put J_2(t_0)=2(1/3+t_0²). Its exact numerator is

    4I_2−8βh+β²J_2(t_0).

For each β this positive numerator is minimized over s by s=0. The minimizing tilt is

    β_*=4h/J_2(t_0)=2h/(1/3+t_0²),

which satisfies |β_*|≤6|h|<1/4. Completing the square now gives (16). Exterior directions remain strictly above γ while this local value is at most γ, so the formula is global over all cap directions in the stated source interval. In particular the missing vertical direction is constrained quadratically, even though every active cap gradient is horizontal.

## 6. The actual failure of active-normal qualification

The ordinary centroid of K_ε has horizontal component zero and height

    g_t=(2ε/3)/(1+ε²/3)>ε/3=t_*.

The finite affine symmetries permuting the vertices of T preserve K_ε and fix y_*. Uniqueness of the projective energy minimizer therefore forces its horizontal parameter to be zero: the only horizontal covector invariant under all these symmetries is zero. Its vertical parameter is nonzero, since the zero parameter minimizes the energy exactly at the ordinary centroid. In fact it is positive, because the vertical derivative of the parameter objective at zero is −4|K_ε|(g_t−t_*)<0 and that one-dimensional objective is strictly convex.

By the established energy envelope formula, the spatial energy gradient at y_* is 4 E_(K_ε)(y_*) times that parameter, a nonzero vertical vector. The gradient of its cube root is a positive multiple of the same vector. Neither lies in the horizontal span of (1).

The deepest-point set is the singleton {y_*}, so y_* maximizes the secondary energy on that set. Nevertheless NO nonnegative combination, nor even signed combination, of the actual active halfspace normals can represent its secondary gradient. This directly falsifies an unqualified finite active-normal KKT conclusion for this actual depth problem. It does not contradict a closed normal-cone or limiting-constraint statement: the near-active tilted caps encode the quadratic restriction (16).

For clarity, an actual mixed version uses C=[0,1]_z×K_ε, with exactly two integer fibers at z=0,1. At either base the best continuous mark is y_*, and the deepest normalized mixed depth is γ/2=2/9. Every containing ambient halfspace captures at least the own-fiber ordinary fraction γ; conversely a sufficiently large finite base tilt excludes the other fiber and realizes any chosen own cap. Thus these claims are exact. At a critical mixed cap the own fraction must be γ and the other fiber must contribute zero, so ALL critical continuous normals are again the horizontal normals (1). The vertical own-energy gradient is still outside their cone. This product body is fully OC-safe; its role is solely the qualification obstruction.
